missions.title: The Label on the Blade
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What do we need to know about how something was made before we can say what it is?

objectives.title: Arrive in Emberford, a guild town in Aethelgard.
Find out what the trader Corvan claims about his patterned blade.
Gather at least three pieces of evidence about how the blade was made (smith, guild, scholar, assay table).
At Hesper's forge, sort the process steps: pattern welding, crucible steel, or both.
Go back to Corvan and decide what to do about the blade and its label.
Report to Kip by the portal stone.

cards.title: Corvan's sign
cards.text: Corvan's sign says: 'True wootz of ancient Damascus. 24 marks.'
cards.limits: A seller's description is a claim. It is not a record of how the blade was made or where it came from.

cards.title: Hesper's workshop sheet
cards.text: Hesper's sheet for this blade: layers of two different steels stacked, forge-welded, twisted and folded, then shaped and etched. Dated this season.
cards.limits: This is the maker's own record. It does not say where her steel stock came from.

cards.title: Assay cross-section (schematic)
cards.text: The assay table's etched cross-section shows separate welded layers that follow the folds of the blade.
cards.limits: In this game it is a schematic illustration, not a real micrograph. A trained assayer would need to confirm it.

cards.title: Guild ledger entry
cards.text: Emberford guild ledger: one patterned blade sold by the Lyle workshop to Corvan Hale, this season.
cards.limits: The ledger records a sale. It does not describe the steel.

cards.title: Ten wootz steel ingots (Met record)
cards.text: The Metropolitan Museum of Art catalogues 'Ten Wootz Steel Ingots with Bag', accession 2023.133a–k, as Indian, probably eighteenth century.
cards.limits: The word 'probably' is part of the record. These are ingots, the raw material, not finished blades.

cards.title: Met essay on techniques
cards.text: The Met's essay on decorating arms and armour separates pattern welding, which joins and works different iron or steel pieces, from crucible or 'watered' steel.
cards.limits: An essay about techniques does not identify any particular blade.

cards.title: Two kinds of 'Damascus'
cards.text: A 1998 experimental study by Verhoeven, Pendray and Dauksch uses both 'pattern-welded Damascus' and 'wootz Damascus'. So 'Damascus' alone does not name one recipe.
cards.limits: The study examines particular wootz blades. It says nothing about blades sold in Emberford.

claims.text: The blade is true wootz from ancient Damascus.
The blade was pattern-welded in Hesper's workshop this season.
A patterned surface alone does not show that steel is wootz.

exhibits.name: Patterned blade on Corvan's stall
exhibits.dateKind: A SELLER'S CLAIM, not a date from any record. Nothing on the stall says when or where it was made.
exhibits.summary: A blade with a wavy, layered surface pattern. In this game world it was made in Emberford. It is NOT a historical object and has no ancient provenance.
exhibits.altText: A short steel blade with a flowing grey pattern of light and dark bands on its surface.

exhibits.name: Ten Wootz Steel Ingots with Bag (catalogue record, Met 2023.133a–k)
exhibits.dateKind: A CATALOGUE DATE with a qualifier. 'Probably' means the museum is not certain. Keep the qualifier.
exhibits.summary: Sefa's catalogue shows the record of a real group of ten wootz steel ingots with a bag, catalogued by The Metropolitan Museum of Art as Indian, probably eighteenth century.
exhibits.altText: A catalogue page showing ten small rounded dark metal cakes next to a cloth bag.

exhibits.name: Assay table: etched cross-section
exhibits.dateKind: A PREPARATION DATE: when this test sample was cut and etched.
exhibits.summary: An offcut from the same billet as Corvan's blade, cut and etched by the guild assayer. The drawing is schematic.
exhibits.altText: A small polished steel slice with bands of light and dark layers that bend along folds.

journal.text: Emberford, Aethelgard. A trader sells a 'true wootz' blade. My job: find out what is known about how it was made.
Corvan says the blade is 'true wootz of ancient Damascus'. He bought it in good faith, he says, and the pattern 'proves it'.
Hesper says she made the blade this season by pattern welding. She is proud of the work and wants it named for what it is.
Sefa: 'Damascus' can mean pattern-welded or wootz steel. Wootz is a crucible-steel tradition. A pattern alone does not show which.
I sorted the process steps. Shaping and etching belong to both routes, so a patterned surface cannot tell them apart on its own.
The guild ledger records the sale from the Lyle workshop to Corvan this season.
I bought the blade at a fair price with an honest label: 'Pattern-welded, Lyle workshop, this season.'
I paid the full price and kept the seller's label, but annotated my own record: pattern-welded, made this season.
I posted a correction on the guild board. Buyers are protected; Corvan lost face.
I did not buy the blade and left the label to Corvan. The question stays open in the market.
Field mission complete. A label is a claim. Before naming what something is, I need to know how it was made and who says so.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: Guardians! Look at this. True wootz of ancient Damascus. See the water in the steel? Only twenty-four marks.

options.text: How do you know it is wootz?

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: The pattern! Everyone knows Damascus steel has that pattern. I'm not a smith, but I know what I see.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: A local workshop sold it to me. They didn't say much. I assumed old stock. I paid fair, and I have a family to feed.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: Isn't it? Look closer if you like. The blade is on the stall.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: Still thinking? The blade won't stay here forever.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: Back again. You've been asking around about my blade. So what will it be?

options.text: Pay 12 marks, and relabel it honestly: 'Pattern-welded, Lyle workshop, this season.'
Pay the full 24 marks. Keep his label, but annotate my own record.
Post a correction on the guild board for all buyers.
Don't buy it. Leave the label to Corvan.
What did Hesper say about it, again?

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: You talked to Hesper? ...Fine. She made it. This season. I thought 'Damascus' was just what you call steel that looks like that. Maybe it isn't.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: Twelve, with Hesper's name on the label. Less than I hoped. But it is honest, and her name might sell the next one.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: Twenty-four it is! A pleasure. What you write in your own book is your business.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: On the board? For everyone to read? ...You may be right about the steel. You did not have to make it so public.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: Your choice. The next buyer may not ask so many questions.

dialogue.speaker: merchant-corvan
dialogue.text: Business goes on. Mind how you go, Guardian.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: That blade on Corvan's stall? I made it. This season, in this forge. Pattern-welded: two steels, stacked, welded, twisted and folded.

options.text: Does that make it worse than wootz?
Can I try sorting the steps?

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: Is that a museum label in your bag? 'Who did what, and when.' Good. Then you'll want my workshop sheet. I made that blade, this season, by pattern welding.

options.text: Can I try sorting the steps?

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: Worse? No. Different. It's good steel and good work. But it is not wootz and it is not ancient. I want it called what it is.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: I sold it to Corvan with my sheet. He didn't keep the sheet. Traders and makers want different things from a label.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: The process cards are on the anvil bench. Schematic only. No real recipe. Sort them into pattern welding, crucible steel, or both.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: The process cards are on the anvil bench whenever you want them. Some steps happen in both kinds of steelmaking. Watch for those.

dialogue.speaker: smith-hesper
dialogue.text: Whatever you decided, you asked the maker first. Most people don't.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: The trade ledger? Every sale in Emberford goes in it. A copy costs 3 marks, unless you carry a registry letter.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: A Nexus registry letter. Venn's hand, I'd know it anywhere. No charge. Here: Lyle workshop to Corvan Hale, one patterned blade, this season.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: Thank you. Here: Lyle workshop to Corvan Hale, one patterned blade, this season.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: The guild keeps trade peaceful. A quiet correction is usually better than a loud one. But that is a guild view.

dialogue.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
dialogue.text: The market will remember how this was handled, one way or another.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: A Guardian! I carry museum catalogues from your world. You're looking into the word 'Damascus'? It's a slippery word.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: Wootz is a historical crucible-steel tradition. Not every crucible steel is wootz. And a pattern on the surface does not prove that a blade is wootz.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: Here: the Met's record for ten wootz steel ingots with a bag. Catalogued as Indian, 'probably' eighteenth century. Keep the 'probably'. Open my catalogue on the table to read it.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: Ask, and I'll check my prepared topics.

dialogue.speaker: scholar-sefa
dialogue.text: My catalogue is on the table. And you can still ask me a question of your own.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: Emberford! Smell that forge. Talk to Corvan at the striped stall first. Then the smith, the guild hall, and the scholar by the fountain.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: So? What did you decide about the blade? Come to the portal stone and tell me properly.

options.text: Here is what I found and what I decided.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: A label is a claim. You checked who made it, how, and when, before deciding. Let's report back to Warden Ise.

dialogue.speaker: kip-arden
dialogue.text: That was a good first week. I wonder what the Nexus will send us next.

dialogue.speaker: villager-1
dialogue.text: Ember tea? One mark. It doesn't make you smarter, but it makes the walk nicer.

dialogue.speaker: villager-1
dialogue.text: Enjoy. Mind the forge sparks.

hints.text: You are arriving in Emberford.
Wait for the portal to finish.
Arrival completes this step.
If nothing happens, walk a step. Arrival is recorded when you move.
The trader Corvan has a striped stall in the market.
Ask Corvan what he says the blade is, and how he knows.
A seller's claim is a starting point. Note it, then look for other evidence.
Walk to the blue-and-white striped stall and talk to Corvan (red shirt).
Several people in Emberford know something about the blade.
Who made it? Who recorded the sale? What do scholars say the words mean? What does the steel itself show?
Different kinds of evidence check each other: a maker's record, a sales record, a test sample and a scholarly account.
Talk to Hesper at the forge (west), Guildmaster Orrin at the guild hall (north), Sefa by the fountain, or open the assay table. Any three count.
Hesper's anvil bench has process cards to sort.
Some steps belong to only one route. Some belong to both.
Pattern welding joins different pieces. Crucible steel is melted in a sealed pot. Shaping and etching happen in both.
Put 'stack', 'forge-weld' and 'twist' under pattern welding; 'seal', 'melt' and 'cool to ingot' under crucible; 'shape' and 'etch' under both.
Corvan is waiting for your decision.
Each choice affects Corvan, Hesper, the guild and future buyers differently.
There is no hidden correct choice. Choose one you can support with your evidence, and notice what it costs.
Talk to Corvan at the striped stall and pick one of the options.
Kip is waiting by the portal stone.
Tell Kip what you found.
The game saves a checkpoint when you report.
Walk to the glowing stone in the south of town and talk to Kip.
